name: Codeine
summary: A weak mu-opioid agonist that is essentially a prodrug: analgesia depends on CYP2D6 conversion to morphine, making its effect highly variable and now contraindicated in children.
mechanism: Prodrug — O-demethylated by CYP2D6 to morphine, the main active analgesic; codeine itself is a weak mu-opioid agonist.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP2D6 to morphine; CYP3A4 to norcodeine); ~10% of dose converted to morphine

dosing.adult: 30–60 mg PO q4–6h PRN; combination products are limited by the paracetamol co-ingredient
dosing.renalAdjustment: Reduce dose in severe renal impairment

safety.pregnancy: Avoid for analgesia where alternatives exist; chronic use causes neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome
warnings: Black box: addiction, abuse, and misuse — risk of opioid use disorder
Black box: accidental ingestion and overdose (especially in children) can be fatal
Black box: neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome with prolonged use during pregnancy
CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers rapidly convert codeine to morphine — fatal respiratory depression reported; ultrarapid and poor metabolizers make analgesia unpredictable
Contraindicated in children <12 years and after pediatric tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy
monitoring: Respiratory status — especially in children (contraindicated) and ultrarapid metabolizers
Paracetamol co-ingestion limits in combination products
Pain response — poor response may signal poor CYP2D6 metabolism
safety.overdose: Respiratory depression, coma, miosis; naloxone reverses opioid effects

indications: Mild to moderate pain (usually in combination with paracetamol)
clinicalPearls: A prodrug — without CYP2D6 activity there is essentially no analgesia; this genetic variability is why codeine is now contraindicated in children
The ~10% morphine conversion creates an analgesic ceiling — combination products are the usual vehicle
good: Mild pain and cough in adults when simple analgesics fail (where available).
bad: Children under 12, breastfeeding mothers, poor or ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers, and anyone needing reliable opioid analgesia.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard neurology/pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
